newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, Chirac to discuss NATO's plans.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, Chirac to discuss NATO's plans.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, who is recovering from pneumonia, is due to meet French President Jaques Chirac on Sunday for talks dominated by Russia's worries about NATO's plans to expand eastwards.

Yeltsin and Chirac, his first foreign guest since he left hospital on January 20, are scheduled to hold 2 1/2 hours of talks in the government residence Novo-Ogaryovo 20 km (13 miles) west of Moscow, Interfax news agency said.

Yeltsin, who turned 66 on Saturday, is also likely to use the talks as another chance to show that he fully controls Russia despite health problems which kept him away from the Kremlin for most of time since his re-election in July.

Interfax quoted government experts as saying that the two leaders would discuss prospects of promoting stronger bilateral trade and economic links and creating a better climate for French investments in Russia.
But they predicted that the talks would focus on NATO's plans to grant full NATO membership to Moscow's former Cold War allies in Eastern Europe.

Russia insists that NATO's expansion would threaten its security and cause new divisions in Europe. Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing on Friday that Moscow was consistent in its opposition to the enlargement.

But, after NATO made clear that Russia's objections would not stop its expansion, Moscow appears to have switched to negotiating a deal which would keep the alliance's military structures away from its borders.
Government officials say Russia is seeking a binding document rather than a political declaration.
They say that in an ideal world this document should include a promise not to deploy nuclear forces, heavy weapons and troops belonging to other NATO countries on the territory of the new members.
Moscow is clearly looking for support from within NATO, especially from some of its European members who seek to take over some alliance command functions from the United States.
Government officials have said that Moscow closely watched debates between Washington and Paris about whether an American or European should command NATO's southern flank.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin and Chirac would "compare approaches to the creation of a new security architecture in Europe."
"We have much in common on this respect," he said. "NATO will also be discussed. As you know, the position of France differs somewhat from that of Washington and Bonn."

A French official has said that Paris supported Moscow's demands for a binding charter on Russia-NATO relations and felt the United States was still trying to fob off the Russians with a few, non-binding pledges.
Washington and most NATO allies oppose a legally binding accord requiring parliamentary ratification.
Chirac hopes NATO can work out a deal with Russia before an alliance summit in Madrid in July at which it is expected to issue invitations to some eastern European states.
